sentences.text: Bistahieversor is a genus containing only one known species, B. sealeyi, which was described in 2010 from Late Cretaceous rocks in New Mexico.
Adult Bistahieversor are estimated to have reached a length of about 9 meters and weighed at least one ton.
A 2016 study by Molina-Pérez and Larramendi estimated the length of Bistahieversor at 9 meters and its weight at 3.3 metric tons.
A complete skull and partial skeleton found in the Bisti/De-Na-Zin Wilderness Area of New Mexico in 1998 are colloquially known as the "Bisti Beast".
The extra opening above the eye in Bistahieversor is thought to have housed an air sac that would have reduced the skull's weight.
The first remains attributed to Bistahieversor were originally described in 1990 as a specimen of the genus Aublysodon.
The genus name Bistahieversor is derived from the Navajo word for the Bisti/De-Na-Zin Wilderness Area, meaning "place of the adobe formations".
The specific epithet 'eversor' in the name Bistahieversor means "destroyer" in Latin.
Bistahieversor possessed a complex joint at its forehead designed to stabilize the skull and prevent movement at that joint.
Large olfactory bulbs in Bistahieversor indicate a heightened sense of smell, while elongated semi-circular canals suggest increased agility and sophisticated gaze stabilization.
Although Bistahieversor had small optic lobes, this feature is not considered a strong indicator of poor vision in the dinosaur.
Geographical barriers such as the formation of the Rocky Mountains may have isolated southern Bistahieversor populations from more advanced northern tyrannosaurs.
Bistahieversor is often classified within the subfamily Tyrannosaurinae as a derived tyrannosaur.
Bistahieversor lived during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 75 million years ago in the Campanian stage, in what is now North America.
A 2024 reanalysis by Rivera-Sylva & Longrich, based on new data, placed Bistahieversor within the tyrannosaurine clade Teratophoneini alongside Labocania, Dynamoterror, and Teratophoneus.
A 2025 study by Zanno and Napoli recovered Bistahieversor as a basal representative of the Albertosaurinae subfamily alongside Jinbeisaurus.
